key_terms.meaning: A band-limited signal with highest frequency f_max is fully represented by samples taken at f_s > 2f_max.
The minimum sampling rate 2f_max for a signal band-limited to f_max.
The maximum sample spacing 1/(2f_max) that avoids loss of information.
Passing an impulse-sampled signal through an ideal low-pass filter with cutoff f_s/2 rebuilds the original band-limited signal.
Reconstruction x(t)=Σ x(nT) sinc((t−nT)/T), where sinc(u)=sin(πu)/(πu) and T=1/f_s.
Overlap of spectral replicas when f_s ≤ 2f_max; high frequencies appear as false low frequencies.
An analog low-pass filter placed before the sampler to remove frequencies above f_s/2.
A narrow band from f_L to f_H can be sampled below 2f_H if the alias bands are placed outside the signal band.
A practical sampler that holds each sample for an aperture time τ, producing a sinc attenuation in frequency.
The sinc envelope sin(πfτ)/(πfτ) from finite sampling pulse width reduces high-frequency amplitude.
Rounding each sample to one of 2^n levels for an n-bit representation.
For a uniform quantizer, Δ=(x_max−x_min)/2^n with n bits.
The rounding error e[n] is modelled as additive noise uniform in [−Δ/2, Δ/2] with variance Δ²/12.
h[n] is the output of a discrete-time LTI system to input δ[n]; it fully characterizes the system.
y[n]=Σ_{k=−∞}^{∞} x[k]h[n−k] gives the output of an LTI system with input x[n] and impulse response h[n].
y[n]+Σ_{k=1}^N a_k y[n−k]=Σ_{m=0}^M b_m x[n−m] relates output and input samples.
Roots of the denominator polynomial of H(z); their locations decide stability and natural response.
A causal LTI system is stable if and only if all poles lie strictly inside the unit circle |z|<1.
A system whose output depends on past output samples as well as input samples.
A system whose output depends only on present and past input samples, giving an FIR form.

takeaways: Sampling above the Nyquist rate preserves a band-limited signal; sampling below it creates irreversible aliasing.
An anti-aliasing filter must act before the sampler; digital filtering after sampling cannot remove aliases.
Band-pass sampling can use a rate below twice the top frequency when the signal bandwidth is narrow.
Sample-and-hold introduces sinc attenuation called the aperture effect, which can be compensated by inverse sinc filtering.
Quantization adds noise with variance Δ²/12, and each extra bit lowers quantization noise by about 6 dB.
A discrete-time LTI system is fully specified by h[n], and its output is the convolution sum x[n]*h[n].
Difference equations compute outputs recursively, and pole positions inside the unit circle give stability.
Sampling links continuous and discrete time through x[n]=x(nT), while reconstruction restores x(t) under the sampling condition.
bank_note: Long answers tend to combine the sampling theorem with aliasing and practical reconstruction, then test convolution-sum and difference-equation analysis; keep derivations, spectral sketches and stability conditions ready.

bank.q: State the sampling theorem for a band-limited signal and derive the ideal reconstruction formula using sinc interpolation.
outline: Define f_max and a band-limited signal.
Show the spectrum of the impulse-sampled signal has replicas at multiples of f_s.
State the condition f_s > 2f_max.
Write x(t)=Σ x(nT) sinc((t−nT)/T).
Explain the ideal low-pass reconstruction filter with cutoff f_s/2.

bank.q: Explain aliasing using the spectrum of a sampled signal. Define Nyquist rate and Nyquist frequency with an example.
outline: Draw the baseband spectrum and its replicas.
Show overlap when f_s < 2f_max.
Define Nyquist rate as 2f_max and Nyquist frequency as f_s/2.
Give one numerical alias example.
State that aliasing is irreversible after sampling.

bank.q: Define uniform quantization. Derive the step size and show that quantization noise variance is Δ²/12 for a uniform error model.
outline: Define n-bit uniform quantization.
Write Δ=(x_max−x_min)/2^n.
Model error e as uniform in [−Δ/2, Δ/2].
Compute mean zero and variance Δ²/12.
State the assumptions of the noise model.

bank.q: Define a discrete-time LTI system and derive its convolution-sum output from the impulse response.
outline: Define linearity and time invariance in discrete time.
Write x[n]=Σ x[k]δ[n−k].
Use superposition and time invariance.
Obtain y[n]=Σ x[k]h[n−k].
State commutativity and other basic properties.

bank.q: A signal x(t)=3 cos(2π1000t)+2 cos(2π3500t) is sampled at f_s=4 kHz. Find the alias frequencies and explain whether the original signal can be recovered.
outline: Nyquist frequency is 2 kHz.
1000 Hz lies below Nyquist and remains at 1000 Hz.
3500 Hz aliases to 500 Hz because 3500−4000=−500.
Original signal cannot be recovered because 3500 Hz is above Nyquist.
State that an anti-aliasing filter before the sampler was needed.

bank.q: A signal has frequency components at 500 Hz, 1.8 kHz and 2.6 kHz. Choose a sampling rate and specify an anti-aliasing filter. Explain your choice.
outline: f_max=2.6 kHz, so f_s must exceed 5.2 kHz.
Choose a convenient rate such as 8 kHz.
Set anti-aliasing low-pass cutoff between 2.6 kHz and f_s/2.
Explain that the filter removes components above f_s/2 before sampling.
Check no component aliases into the desired band.

bank.q: For h[n]=a^n u[n] with |a|<1, compute y[n]=x[n]*h[n] when x[n]=u[n]−u[n−5].
outline: Write the convolution sum y[n]=Σ x[k]h[n−k].
Use the finite support of x[k] from k=0 to 4.
Insert h[n−k]=a^{n−k}u[n−k].
Split cases by n and use a finite geometric series.
Give the piecewise output and check the limit for large n.

bank.q: Solve y[n]−0.5y[n−1]=x[n] with zero initial condition for x[n]=u[n]; state whether the system is stable.
outline: Start from y[n]=0.5y[n−1]+u[n].
Compute the first few samples or use the geometric sum.
Obtain y[n]=2(1−0.5^{n+1}) for n≥0.
Identify the pole at z=0.5.
Since |0.5|<1, the causal system is stable.

bank.q: A uniform quantizer with n=8 bits covers −5 V to +5 V. Find the step size, quantization noise power, and rms error.
outline: Compute Δ=0.0390625 V.
Noise power is Δ²/12≈1.27×10⁻⁴ V².
rms error is sqrt(Δ²/12)≈0.0113 V.
State the uniform-error assumption.

bank.q: A band-pass signal occupies 20 kHz to 24 kHz. Derive a valid band-pass sampling rate below 2×24 kHz and check that aliases do not fall inside the band.
outline: Use f_L=20 kHz, f_H=24 kHz, B=4 kHz.
Use the band-pass condition 2f_H/m ≤ f_s ≤ 2f_L/(m−1).
Choose m=3, giving 16 kHz ≤ f_s ≤ 20 kHz.
Pick f_s=18 kHz as a valid rate.
Check that translated bands do not overlap 20–24 kHz.

bank.q: Compare ideal sinc reconstruction with zero-order hold reconstruction. Derive the aperture-effect sinc factor and discuss a compensation method.
outline: Explain ideal low-pass reconstruction and its sinc kernel.
Model zero-order hold by a rectangular pulse.
Derive the sinc factor sin(πfτ)/(πfτ).
Discuss high-frequency attenuation and phase effects.
Suggest inverse sinc equalization or a smaller aperture.

bank.q: A sampled system shows a false 300 Hz tone when the input contains a 3.7 kHz component. Determine a possible sampling frequency, explain the alias, and specify the anti-aliasing filter.
outline: Try f_s=4 kHz.
The alias is |3700−4000|=300 Hz.
Explain folding about multiples of f_s.
An anti-aliasing low-pass filter before the sampler must remove 3.7 kHz.
Set cutoff below 2 kHz for f_s=4 kHz.

bank.q: For a second-order difference equation with poles at z=0.8 and z=−0.6, discuss stability and natural response. What changes if a pole moves to z=1.2?
outline: Both poles lie inside the unit circle, so the causal system is stable.
Natural response contains terms proportional to 0.8^n and (−0.6)^n.
Both terms decay as n increases.
A pole at z=1.2 lies outside the unit circle.
The system becomes unstable and the response grows.

bank.q: Analyse an end-to-end chain: analog anti-aliasing filter, sampler, n-bit quantizer, discrete-time LTI filter, and reconstruction filter. Explain how each block affects aliasing, quantization noise, and stability, and give design trade-offs.
outline: Anti-aliasing filter limits input bandwidth before sampling.
Sampler must satisfy the Nyquist condition or aliasing appears.
n-bit quantizer adds noise of variance Δ²/12.
Discrete-time LTI filter shapes signal and noise and must be stable.
Reconstruction filter removes spectral replicas and smooths the output.
Trade-offs include filter order, sampling rate, word length and cost.

glossary.def: The process of taking values of a continuous-time signal at discrete instants.
A signal whose Fourier transform is zero above some highest frequency f_max.
Half the sampling rate, f_s/2; it is the highest frequency that can be represented without aliasing.
The minimum sampling rate 2f_max for a signal band-limited to f_max.
Recovering a continuous-time signal from its samples, usually by low-pass filtering.
sinc(u)=sin(πu)/(πu), with sinc(0)=1; it is the ideal interpolation kernel.
A copy of the signal spectrum shifted by multiples of the sampling frequency f_s.
A false low-frequency component produced when spectral replicas overlap.
An analog low-pass filter placed before a sampler to limit the input bandwidth.
An unused frequency interval between the signal band and the Nyquist frequency or filter transition band.
Sampling a narrow high-frequency band at a rate lower than twice its top frequency.
A circuit that samples an input and holds the value for an aperture time.
The duration for which a sampler holds or averages the input sample.
Mapping continuous sample amplitudes to a finite set of levels.
A quantizer with equal step size Δ between adjacent levels.
The difference between the actual sample value and the quantized value; it is modelled as noise.
The ratio of signal power to quantization noise power; it improves by about 6 dB per extra bit.
A sequence x[n] defined only at integer indices n.
δ[n]=1 at n=0 and 0 otherwise; it is the identity for convolution.
The output h[n] of an LTI system to the unit impulse δ[n].
y[n]=Σ x[k]h[n−k], the output of a discrete-time LTI system.
An equation relating the current output sample to past outputs and present or past inputs.
H(z)=Y(z)/X(z) for an LTI system, the ratio of Z-transforms of output and input.
A value of z that makes the denominator of H(z) zero; it controls the natural response and stability.
Every bounded input gives a bounded output; for a causal LTI system, all poles must lie inside the unit circle.
A reconstruction method that holds each sample constant until the next sample.
